title: Rule of Thirds in Photography: The Grid and When to Break It — cv.cm
description: The rule of thirds explained: where to put eyes, horizons and subjects on the 3x3 grid, how to turn on grid lines on a phone, and when to center instead.
h1: What is the rule of thirds in photography?
answer: The rule of thirds divides the frame into a 3x3 grid with two horizontal and two vertical lines. You place the main subject on a line or near one of the four crossing points instead of in the center, and put the horizon on the top or bottom line. It gives the eye somewhere to travel and usually feels more balanced than a centered shot.

body: Imagine two lines that cut the picture into three equal parts from left to right, and two more that cut it into three equal parts from top to bottom. You now have nine boxes and four points where the lines cross. Camera makers often call these crossing points the strong points or hot spots of the frame.

The guideline is simple: put the thing you want people to look at on one of those lines or close to one of the four points. It does not need to sit exactly on the point. Close is enough, because viewers do not measure, they only feel whether the picture is balanced.

ul: Main subject: near one of the four crossing points.
Horizon: on the upper line (to show more land or water) or the lower line (to show more sky).
Tall subjects such as a person standing, a tree or a tower: along one of the vertical lines.
Eyes in a portrait: on or near the upper horizontal line.
Empty space: on the side the subject faces or moves toward.

sections.h: Why off-center placement often works better
body: When the subject sits in the exact middle, the eye goes straight to it and stops. When the subject is a third of the way in, the eye moves between the subject and the space around it, so the picture feels more active. The empty part of the frame is not wasted. It shows where the subject is, where it is looking, or where it is going.

The horizon rule follows the same logic. A horizon across the middle splits the picture into two equal halves that compete with each other. Moving it to a third line tells the viewer which half matters. If the sky has dramatic clouds, give it two thirds. If the sky is flat and white, give the land or water two thirds and keep the sky small.

Direction matters too. A person looking to the right should usually be placed on the left vertical line, so they look into the open part of the frame. A runner or a car moving left should be on the right line, with space ahead. Photographers call this lead room or looking room. Without it, the subject seems to press against the edge.

body.note: The rule of thirds is a starting point, not a law. Use it when you are unsure where to put something, and check the result on the screen.

sections.h: How to turn on grid lines on a phone or camera
body: Almost every phone and camera can show the 3x3 grid on the screen. It is not saved in the photo. It only helps you place things while you shoot, and it also helps you keep horizons and buildings straight.

head: Device
Where to find the grid
Notes
rows: iPhone
Settings app > Camera > Grid (and Level)
The setting is in the Settings app, not inside the Camera app.
Google Pixel
Camera app > Settings > More settings > Grid type
Choose the 3x3 grid. Other grid types exist but 3x3 is the rule of thirds.
Other Android phones
Camera app > Settings (gear icon) > Grid lines
Names vary by maker. Search the camera settings for grid.
Mirrorless or DSLR camera
Menu > Display or Shooting display > Grid display
Often several grids are offered. Pick 3x3 or the one marked rule of thirds.

body: Turn on the level as well if your device offers one. A tilted horizon is the most common reason a photo feels wrong even when the subject is placed well.

head: Subject
Where to place it
What to avoid
rows: Head-and-shoulders portrait
Eyes on the upper line; the nearer eye close to an upper crossing point
Eyes in the middle of the frame with a large gap above the head
Full-length portrait
Body along a vertical line; space on the side the person faces
Cutting off feet or hands at the edge
Landscape or seascape
Horizon on the upper or lower line; a tree, rock or boat on a crossing point
Horizon exactly through the middle, or tilted
Sunset
Sun near a lower crossing point; horizon on the lower line if the sky is colorful
A plain sky taking most of the frame
Street or travel
Person walking into the frame from a vertical line
Person walking out of the frame with no space ahead
Food or product
Main item on a crossing point; props along the opposite line
Every item lined up in the center
Animals and pets
Eyes near an upper crossing point; space in the direction they look
Focus or placement on the nose instead of the eyes

body: If you shot with the subject in the middle, you can often move it to a third by cropping. Most phone photo editors show the 3x3 grid while you crop, so you can drag the frame until the subject sits on a line.

ol: Open the photo in your editor and choose Crop.
Decide the final shape first: 4:5 for many social feeds, 1:1 square, 3:2 for prints, 16:9 for screens.
Drag the crop box so the main subject or the eyes land on a line or crossing point.
Straighten the horizon with the rotate or straighten slider while the grid is visible.
Check that you did not cut through hands, feet, or the top of the head at a joint.
Save a copy, not over the original, so you can try again.

body: Cropping removes pixels, so leave some room around the subject when you shoot. A photo framed too tightly cannot be moved to a third later. In a browser, cv.cm's crop tool shows square, 4:5 and 16:9 frames and keeps the photo on your device.

sections.h: When to break the rule of thirds
body: Centering is the right choice more often than many guides admit. Use it on purpose, not by habit.

ul: Symmetry: buildings, bridges, doors, roads and reflections in still water look strongest when the line of symmetry runs through the center.
Strong eye contact: a person looking straight into the lens, centered, feels direct and confident.
Square format: in a 1:1 frame, a centered subject often looks calm and deliberate.
Small subject in a large empty space: a single figure in the middle of a white snow field or a plain wall can be very effective.
Patterns: a repeating pattern that fills the frame does not need a single point of interest.

body: Some photographers prefer the golden ratio, which puts the lines slightly closer to the center (about 38 percent and 62 percent of the width instead of 33 and 67 percent). In practice the difference is small. Either one is better than placing everything by accident.

ul: Placing the subject on a line but leaving it out of focus. On a phone, tap the subject on the screen so focus and exposure follow it, not the center.
Putting a person on the left line but having them face the left edge. Swap sides so they look into the frame.
Using the rule on every photo. A whole set of off-center pictures can look as repetitive as a set of centered ones.
Ignoring what is on the other crossing points. A bright sign or a bin on an empty power point can steal attention from the subject.
Letting the horizon slide. If the horizon is on the lower line on the left and higher on the right, the picture is tilted. Turn on the level.

faq.q: Who invented the rule of thirds?
faq.a: The idea is usually traced to the English painter and engraver John Thomas Smith, who described it in 1797 in a book about landscape painting. Painters used similar off-center placements long before it had a name.

faq.q: Is the rule of thirds the same as the golden ratio?
faq.a: No. The rule of thirds splits the frame into equal thirds. The golden ratio splits it in a ratio of about 1 to 1.618, so its lines sit a little nearer the center. The rule of thirds is a simpler approximation.

faq.q: Does the rule of thirds work for vertical photos?
faq.a: Yes. The grid simply stretches to the new shape. In a vertical portrait the eyes still go on the upper line, and in a vertical landscape the horizon goes on a third line.

faq.q: Should I always put the horizon on a third line?
faq.a: Not always. A reflection in calm water often looks best with the horizon through the middle, because the two halves mirror each other. Otherwise, a third line is a safe default.

faq.q: Why do my photos look boring even with the grid on?
faq.a: Placement alone cannot save a photo with flat light or a messy background. Check the light, the background and the moment as well. Composition works together with those, not instead of them.
